title: Pauri 23, meaning: the ant who remembers
hook: rivers flow into the sea without knowing its size; kings with mountains of wealth are not equal to an ant who remembers (Japji 23)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sound of Pauri 23. Your line was saalaahee: the praisers praise, but haven't grasped how great. Did you praise one person out loud? Today, the same stanza's meaning, and a very small hero. Day two hundred.

Have you ever watched an ant for a whole minute? Get down low on a sidewalk and follow one. It carries a crumb twice its size, loses it, finds it, goes around a pebble, keeps going. It never looks up at the buildings or the traffic. It isn't impressed by anything. It just keeps its one thread. Now picture a king on a golden throne, with vaults of treasure and armies at the gate. If someone asked you which one matters more, you'd probably laugh. Pauri 23 gives an answer that stops the laugh.
screen: `WATCH AN ANT FOR A MINUTE.` → `IT KEEPS ITS ONE THREAD.` → `THE ANT, OR THE KING?`

segments.voice: The stanza began yesterday: the praisers praise, but haven't grasped how great. Now it gives two pictures. The first, in paraphrase: rivers and streams pour into the ocean, but they don't know how big the ocean is. They just flow in. That's us, praising. We're part of something we can't measure, and we pour into it anyway. The second picture turns the world's scale upside down. Kings and emperors, with kingdoms as vast as oceans and wealth piled like mountains, are not equal to an ant, if the ant does not forget the One in its heart. The word for ant is keeRee, one of the smallest living things anyone can see. And the condition is simple: je tis manahu na veesarahi, if it does not forget Him in its mind. The whole weight of the scale rests on that one condition. The Sikh word for that is simran, remembrance, keeping the Name in mind through the day. Pauri 23 says a creature the size of a grain of rice, if it remembers, outweighs every palace. It's not saying wealth is evil. Plenty of Sikhs run businesses and work hard. It's saying what the scale is actually measuring. Not size. Not money. Not how much you understand; the river doesn't understand the sea. Just whether you remember. That's the end of this stretch of Japji: bhareeai hath, as you sow, teerath tap, only the Maker knows, worlds beyond worlds, the praisers, and now the ant. Two hundred days in, it's a good picture to carry. Small, steady, remembering.
screen: `RIVERS DON'T KNOW THE SEA.` · `KINGS WITH MOUNTAINS OF WEALTH.` · `AN ANT WHO DOESN'T FORGET.` · `THE SCALE MEASURES REMEMBERING.` · then, large: `BE THE ANT.`

segments.voice: Watch something small. A leaf moving, a drop on a glass, a bug on the windowsill, a crumb, a flicker of light. If there's nothing, watch the small rise and fall of your own breath. Give it your whole attention, the way the ant gives its whole attention to one crumb. Each time your mind wanders off to bigger things, come back to the small one. The bell holds the time.
Simran, remembrance. Rivers pour into a sea they can't measure; kings with mountains of wealth don't equal an ant that remembers.
Your line: be the ant. Today, pick one small moment, a doorway, a sip of water, a red light, and use it to remember. Day two hundred.

screen: `DAY 200 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: PAURI 24, SOUND: ANT NA SIFTEE.`

howItsDone: Pauri 23 is recited in the morning Japji Sahib; Sikhs practice simran, remembering the Name through the day, and often quote the ant of this stanza to say remembrance matters more than wealth or rank.

myth: it says what the scale measures: not size or money, but remembering.
in Pauri 23, an ant who remembers outweighs kings
if it does not forget the One in its heart.
the rivers in Pauri 23 know how big the sea is
they pour in without knowing its size.

fork.setup: on one side, a king with mountains of wealth. on the other, an ant. what does Pauri 23 say tips the scale?
options: the ant, if it doesn't forget the One.
fork.reveal: keeRee tul na hovanee je tis manahu na veesarahi: kings are not equal to an ant, if it does not forget Him in its mind.

original.note: Gurmukhi: keeRee, an ant (the r is said with the tongue curled back); the small hero of Japji Pauri 23.

trapdoor: what you thought: small things don't matter.
what it means: the smallest creature that remembers the One outweighs the greatest wealth.
what a scholar hears: keeRee tul na hovanee, not equal to an ant; the condition, na veesarahi, not forgetting, is the root idea of simran.

notes: Closes the part pauris 20–23; the teach names that part's lines (days 193–199).
Transliteration keeRee (ਕੀੜੀ) and quoted line 'je tis manahu na veesarahi'; confirm.
Link of na veesarahi (not forgetting) to simran is interpretive; confirm.
Audit (second sample): the review no longer says 'day two hundred' twice in a row, and the slogan 'remembering is everything' became a plain statement of the stanza's one condition.
